extracted.intended_audience: laypersons, household members, bystanders, and untrained first-responders (sailors, travelers, ranchers, miners) who may need to give first aid
extracted.subtask_description: Practical first-aid procedures for restoring apparently drowned persons and treating heat-related emergencies (heat exhaustion, heat stroke, sunstroke), plus presentation guidance for lay-oriented medical literature. Includes step-by-step rescue, artificial respiration (team and single-rescuer methods), post-resuscitation care, and heat illness triage and treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arouse the patient (Rule I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not move the patient unless in danger of freezing; instantly expose the face to the air, toward the wind if there be any; wipe dry the mouth and nostrils; rip the clothing so as to expose the chest and waist; give two or three quick, smarting slaps on the chest with the open hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patient does not revive, proceed immediately to the subsequent rules (expel water, produce breathing). Keep drying/rubbing the limbs upward toward the body and apply warmth while not interfering with breathing measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: To expel water from the stomach and chest (Rule II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate the jaws and keep them apart by placing between the teeth a cork or small bit of wood; turn the patient on his face with a large bundle of tightly rolled clothing beneath the stomach; press heavily on the back over it for half a minute or as long as fluids flow freely from the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an initial mechanical means to free the air passages; illustrations (Fig. 1) show patient face down with roll under stomach. After evacuating fluids, proceed to breathing-restoration maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: To produce breathing — team method (Rule III)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combination of the Sylvester and Howard methods: Clear mouth and throat of mucus; turn patient on back with a roll under pit of stomach; draw and hold the tongue forward; one assistant draws the patient's arms upward to enlarge chest capacity; another (astride the hips) uses hands on either side of pit of stomach to press forward and downward to effect expiration, holding pressure about five seconds and then suddenly releasing to allow inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence: arms up (inspiration aided), then arms down and abdominal/chest pressure for expiration; repeat deliberately 12–15 times per minute to imitate natural breathing. If no restoration after about four minutes, turn patient on stomach again to free remaining water and continue artificial respiration for one to four hours or until breathing returns. Continue drying, rubbing, warming (hot flannels, hot-water bottles) concurrently. The combination aims for deepest inspiration (Sylvester) and most complete expiration (Howard).

rubrics_metrics.name: After treatment — external and internal (Rule IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Externally: Strip patient of wet clothing, wrap in blankets, put to bed comfortably warm with free fresh air, and leave to rest. Internally: Give whisky or brandy and hot water in doses of a teaspoonful to a tablespoonful every ten or fifteen minutes for the first hour, or other stimulant as available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor for later manifestations — danger of pulmonary congestion after reaction; maintain perfect rest for at least 48 hours. If breathing difficulty occurs later, apply a large mustard plaster over the breast and assist breathing by repeating artificial respiration if patient gasps before mustard takes effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: To produce respiration — single-rescuer modification
rubrics_metrics.description: If alone, place patient on back with shoulders slightly raised; draw the tongue forward and secure it (teeth, or handkerchief tied under chin); grasp arms below elbows and draw them steadily upward by the sides of the head, then lower the arms and press firmly downward and inward on the sides and front of the chest over the lower ribs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat these movements 12–15 times every minute. Tongue must be kept projecting; handkerchief or plug may be used. The movements imitate the team method but are adapted for one rescuer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructions for saving drowning persons by swimming to their relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rescue steps for swimmers: assure the victim loudly; divest or loosen clothes quickly; if victim struggles, keep off a few seconds until quiet; get close, take fast hold of the hair, turn the victim onto his back, pull to float, then both swim on backs toward shore holding the hair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: do not seize a struggling person immediately; take the hair and throw both on backs for flotation; hold hair with one hand while using the other and feet in diving rescues; use air bubbles to locate submerged bodies; beware of outsetting tides — sometimes better to float on back than trying to reach shore. The method can work with multiple victims; the author reports success with up to four. There is little risk of a 'death grasp' according to the guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat exhaustion — First Aid Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 1: Carry patient flat and lay in shade; loosen clothes at neck and waist. Rule 2: Raise head and give (a) teaspoonful of essence of ginger in a glass of hot water, or (b) half a cup of clear hot coffee. Rule 3: Put him to bed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat exhaustion (heat prostration) typically occurs in those weakened by overwork, worry, or poor food exposed to severe heat; signs include weakness, dizziness, pale cool moist skin, feeble rapid pulse, shallow breathing, and lowered temperature (often ~95–96°F). These measures are for immediate first aid while observing and seeking further care if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat stroke — First Aid Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 1: Send for physician. Rule 2: Remove quickly to shady place, loosening clothes on the way. Rule 3: Strip naked and put on a wire mattress or canvas cot if obtainable. Rule 4: Sprinkle with ice water from watering pot or dash from basin. Rule 5: Dip sheet in ice water and tuck it snugly about patient. Rule 6: Sprinkle outside of sheet with ice water; rub body through the sheet with piece of ice; put piece of ice to nape of neck. Rule 7: When temperature falls to 98.5°F put to bed with ice cap on head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heat stroke is a different, more dangerous condition than heat exhaustion: patient becomes suddenly and completely insensible, face flushed, noisy/difficult breathing, strong pulse, bowel temperature may reach 107–110°F; death rate high (30–50%). Immediate cooling and urgent medical attention are essential; avoid delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sunstroke types and diagnostic distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two distinct types: (1) Heat exhaustion/prostration — often in weakened persons, begins with weakness, dizziness, headache, pale cool moist skin, feeble rapid pulse, lowered temperature. (2) Heat stroke — occurs under direct sun or heavy exertion, sudden complete insensibility, flushed face, noisy/difficult breathing, strong pulse, very high body temperature (107–110°F), possible convulsions, high fatality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate because management and prognosis differ: heat exhaustion responds to shade, cooling drinks, rest; heat stroke requires rapid external cooling and physician. Note high risk of prolonged unconsciousness and later sequelae after heat stroke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for lay-oriented medical literature and presentation (Preface / Introductory Note)
rubrics_metrics.description: Volumes intended for lay readers should be clear, nontechnical, fundamental, concise, and guarded by supervision of qualified medical men. Do not supplant the doctor but supplement; emphasize prevention, warn against self-treatment, and caution that first-aid rules are temporary measures where a physician can possibly be obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presentation specifics: begin each article with simple practical 'First-aid Rules' telling the reader exactly what to do; print these rules in light-faced type to distinguish them from ordinary text. Avoid sensational or morbid illustrations; use instructive pictures with helpful captions. Maintain 'utmost caution' and conservatism in recommendations; warn readers repeatedly of the follies of self-treatment and the need to seek skilled advice for serious conditions.
